items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: I remember talking to Jimmy Noon on the way down here... Jimmy, uh, was playing right by an open window. I got to hear it, and at intermission times he'd come out and we had a nice visit.

ctx.x: The, uh, same studio. I'd have to look that up. I looked all that up for Ralph Gleason about, uh, two or three months ago. Ralph had had the idea it was WWL. It wasn't that. Uh, that, uh, that Bunk had made his records for Jean Williams. Jean did make some records at a studio, WSMB, I guess. His—I know, WSMB, in the Maison Blanc's building in 1942. Uh, Woody, uh, I'm not real sure. I don't have the dope at hand right now. It might have been W—WL, which is the Roosevelt Hotel, possibly, at that time. But, uh,…
Well, he probably hadn't lived here since 1918, I guess.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: I also went to see Jimmy Noon about that time and especially the next year or two, around 37 and 38 I remember.

ctx.x: I heard that song as a white religious piece.

Really? A religious group. The oldest record I ever came across was an old Paramount which wasn't anything very jazzy, you might say. a quartet. You know, a sacred quartet. But anyway, to get back to Dodds, I was surprised then, of course, that to me he was somebody famous. Anybody on the Louis Hot Five would be a famous musician. And he even had a sign out in the front. I was surprised that that was in the first big popularity cycle of Benny Goodman had just made his big hit out in California at the Palladium or…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: Before that I'd gone to see people like Jimmy Noon, Johnny Dodds, and Armstrong, and met a few of my favorite New Orleans musicians.

ctx.x: You want to talk about some of these musicians you've encountered in the course of your career now?

Yes, I might talk a little bit. I happened to pick up an old big box at home I have called Notes, and I dug out a few of the notebooks and other things. One package of notes envelope called Jazzmen material that we collected in 1938 when we were working on Jazzmen. Unfortunately then, we not only didn't have tape recording, we didn't have any other recorders. Nobody was hardly recording interviews. When I started out about that time, they were using mostly aluminum blanks there for a while. You had to play with…
